intro: Each panel makes a different kind of pattern visible at an edge, a seam, or a turn in the surface. These are distinct regional practices with living makers and communities.
alt: Microsoft views a black-and-white Mimbres bowl, a black Pueblo pot, a stepped Diné weaving and a bright yarn study.

variants.name: Mimbres pottery
variants.look: A black creature and angular divisions fit within the white interior of a round bowl.
variants.history: Artists of the Mimbres region made distinctive painted pottery in present-day New Mexico. The best-known black-on-white bowls date mainly to about 1000–1150 CE.
variants.when: Study the relation between the bottom of the bowl and the design that reaches toward its rim.
variants.why: A simple high-contrast figure remains clear across the changes of perspective caused by a curved surface.

source.label: Los Angeles County Museum of Art

variants.name: Pueblo pottery
variants.look: On the dark pot, the reflected light makes the shiny and matte bands stand apart.
variants.history: Many Pueblo communities have distinctive pottery traditions. The black-on-black example refers to work developed by Maria and Julian Martinez of San Ildefonso Pueblo in the twentieth century.
variants.when: Study published examples to see how polishing and firing can carry a pattern within a single color.
variants.why: Changes in sheen make the design emerge and recede as the pot or viewer moves.

variants.name: Navajo weaving
variants.look: Colors make a stepped band across tightly woven wool, and the side shows the cloth's edge.
variants.history: Diné weaving developed over centuries and continues today. Wool, trade, shifting markets and family practice have shaped changes in its materials and designs.
variants.when: Look at both a documented textile and its edges when studying how the loom shapes a design.
variants.why: The stepped motif builds on the intersections of threads and makes structure visible.

variants.name: Huichol yarn painting
variants.look: Small colored yarn lines turn and stack around a simple motif.
variants.history: Wixárika artists in Mexico have used yarn and related materials to make images and objects. Modern commercial and fine-art yarn pictures have their own histories alongside ceremonial practices.
variants.when: Use artist-attributed public examples when studying how colored yarn follows the contours of an image.
variants.why: Closely laid lines give the surface a tactile rhythm and can distinguish adjacent areas even when their colors are similar.

source.label: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian

prompt: Educational art style comparison board. Exactly four square panels arranged as a 2×2 grid in stated reading order, hairline neutral dividers. Recurring original character is an adult woman with ash-blonde hair in a neat low bun, four-color square hair clip, black rectangular glasses worn throughout, black blazer over knee-length black sheath dress, blue lanyard, blank badge, white coffee mug with four colored squares. She is a visiting museumgoer, visibly present in a corner of each frame. Artwork gets most of the visual space. Scene list in exact order: Mimbres black-on-white pottery bowl, large geometric divisions with angular black animal in interior, show both rim and image; Pueblo pottery showcase of living craft, burnished black-on-black geometric band on rounded pot, visually distinctive reflected light; Diné (Navajo) weaving textile detail made of tightly spun wool with stepped stripes in muted red, gray and white, show the edge; Wixárika (Huichol) yarn painting technique on a small contemporary study panel of blue and pink yarn loops making a simple nonreligious abstract blossom. Modern visitor only as viewer. No lettering, captions, watermark or ornamental frame.
